opus-5.5.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying SGD is useless. Obviously it's been spectacularly successful, and that's part of what makes this so interesting. The issue is what I'd call representational optimism. There's an assumption in the field that if you scale up, and the network does well on the benchmarks and the loss goes down, then the representation inside must be good too. People assume it's capturing the world in a sensible, well-organized way. I think that assumption deserves a lot more scrutiny than it gets.

What got us thinking about this was going back to Picbreeder. That's the old system where people bred images by picking ones they liked, and the images came from little networks called CPPNs. When you look inside those evolved networks, you find something remarkable. Take an image like a skull. There's a single connection or node that, when you move it, makes the mouth open and close. Another one controls the symmetry. The representation is modular and factored, in a way that mirrors the actual structure of the thing. Nobody designed it that way. It came out of an open-ended process where people chose stepping stones without aiming at the final image.

Then we asked a simple question. What if you take the exact same image and train a network with conventional SGD to reproduce it, aiming straight at the target? You can get the output to be essentially pixel-perfect, the same image. But when you look inside, it's a mess. We call it fractured, entangled representation, or FER. "Fractured" means that things that should be one concept get split into disconnected pieces handled separately. "Entangled" means that things that should be independent are tangled up together. If you perturb a weight, you don't get "the mouth opens." You get some incoherent smearing across the whole image.

So you have two networks with identical behavior on the objective and totally different internal worlds. That's the core problem. The output metric can't tell you which kind you have. And it matters, because the representation is what determines how you generalize, how you're creative, how you learn the next thing. If what's underneath is fractured and entangled, you may be paying for it in ways the benchmarks hide. You need far more data. You get brittleness in strange places. And you may have a ceiling on real creativity, because you can't make meaningful variations on something you don't represent coherently.

This connects to what Joel Lehman and I have argued for years about objectives. Pushing directly toward an objective is often deceptive. The path that gets you there fastest isn't necessarily the one that builds the right foundations. Picbreeder found those beautiful representations precisely because nobody was optimizing for the skull. They were accumulating stepping stones, things that were interesting in their own right, and the good structure came out of that history. SGD, in its conventional form, is the epitome of greedy objective-driven search. It finds a solution, but not necessarily a good representation of the solution.

So the takeaway isn't "throw away gradient descent." It's that we've been treating loss and performance as a proxy for understanding, and I don't think that's safe. We should be studying representation quality on its own terms. And we should be asking whether ingredients like open-endedness, curricula, and the order in which things are learned can get us the kind of unified, factored representations that we've seen are actually possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that got me thinking about this really started with a very simple experiment. We took a tiny network, just a single image, and we asked: can you learn to output this image? And of course stochastic gradient descent can do that trivially. It learns it in no time. But then we looked inside the network, at what it had actually built in order to represent that image, and it was a mess. It was what I've started calling "fractured entangled representation." The network had found a way to produce the right output, but the internal structure had nothing to do with the structure of the thing it was representing. If the image had symmetry, there was no symmetry inside. If there were parts that were conceptually distinct, those parts were smeared across the whole network, entangled with each other, with the same concept represented in several disconnected places.

And the thing that made this vivid was that we had a comparison. We had networks that had been evolved through open-ended search, through something like Picbreeder, where humans are picking what's interesting and the representation is accumulating over many generations without any objective driving it. And those networks, when they arrived at the same kind of image, had this beautiful, almost crystalline internal structure. You could sweep a single weight and the whole mouth of a face would open and close. The symmetry was there as a single factor. The regularities of the world were literally factored out into separate, clean pieces of the representation.

So the issue isn't that SGD fails to fit the data. It fits the data beautifully. The issue is that it has no reason to care about how it fits the data. Any path down the loss landscape is as good as any other, and the path it finds is this undirected, all-at-once scramble where everything moves together toward the target. There's no principled order to the learning. In the evolved case, the network learned symmetry first, then it learned the rough shape, then it learned the eyes, and every later thing was built on top of the earlier structure. There was a curriculum, in effect, emerging from the process. SGD doesn't have that. It gets everything at once, and so there's no scaffolding, nothing to hang the later concepts on.

And I think this matters because we tend to judge models by their behavior. We say, well, it got the benchmark right, so it understands. But two networks can produce identical outputs and have radically different internal representations, and the quality of that representation is going to determine everything downstream: how well you generalize, how creative you can be, whether you can continue learning without destroying what you already have. A fractured representation is brittle. You move a little bit off distribution and it falls apart, because the thing inside doesn't actually mirror the structure of the world. So my worry is that we've scaled up a paradigm that produces impressive behavior on top of fundamentally impoverished representations, and we haven't been looking at the representations closely enough to notice.

r003.rationale: It says fitting the data need not yield good representations, but does not connect that point to Goodhart’s law.

astra-6.text:
The problem isn’t really SGD as an optimization algorithm. It’s the way we typically frame the task: we define an objective, and then we ask the entire representation to organize itself around improving that objective. That sounds perfectly reasonable, but it assumes that the features worth discovering are the ones that help with the task we can specify right now.

A feature could be interesting or useful in the future without contributing to the current objective. Under conventional SGD, there’s no particular reason to preserve it. It might never emerge, or it might get overwritten as the network becomes better at what we’re asking it to do. So the objective becomes a filter on what the system can discover.

What interests me is whether we can learn representations in a more open-ended way—where discovering something new can be worthwhile even before we know what it’s for. Then a downstream task can draw on that accumulated diversity. Instead of assuming that we already know what a good representation should accomplish, we leave room for useful things to emerge that we wouldn’t have known to ask for.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, by conventional SGD, I mean the setup where you specify an objective and then adjust the weights to get better at that objective. The concern is that we tend to conflate getting better at the objective with learning a better representation of the world. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

A representation can become very good at preserving whatever information is useful for the current task while discarding information that could matter for something else. And once you’ve discarded that information, you may have made future learning harder. So success on the task doesn’t, by itself, tell you that you’re building a foundation for increasingly general capabilities.

That connects to the broader problem with objectives: the stepping stones to something interesting may not look like progress toward it. If every change has to justify itself by reducing the loss right now, you’re constraining which stepping stones you can discover. The question is whether we can build systems that accumulate useful representations in a more open-ended way, where their value doesn’t have to be apparent through one particular objective.
